utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Indah Susanti for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Stanisic Defence, Slobodan Cvijetic and Tatjana Savic and Claire Plumb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So if there are no housekeeping or other preliminary matters, I believe that the witness who was to come has protective measures that we have affirmed, and, therefore, the first thing would be to the lower the blinds before he is escorted to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Would you be so kind as to make the solemn declaration on the card the usher hands to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated. And from your responses, I take it that you are hearing me in a language that you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, welcome to the Tribunal, sir. And I would, first of all, remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- remind you that the solemn declaration that you have just made imposes upon you an obligation to give truthful testimony to the Tribunal, which is empowered to impose penalties for perjury if you give false or misleading testimony. You have been granted the protective measures of a pseudonym and image distortion. The effect of this is that, whereas the -- this being a public trial, insofar as is impracticable, the public, either in the courtroom or listening via the Internet, is able to hear what you're saying, but they would not be able to identify you as the -- as the person who is testifying. So I would, first of all, invite you to look at the pseudonym sheet which the usher will hand to you. And if you're satisfied that it correctly states your name and date of birth, please sign it and hand it back to her. That is admitted under seal and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P01742 [sic], under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sir, you would have previously testified before this Tribunal, and therefore I need only remind you of the procedure that is followed. Namely, that the side calling you - in this case, the Prosecution - begins, and then the side opposite would have questions of you arising out of what the Prosecution has asked. The Prosecution has a right to re-examine, and the Bench may, at that stage or indeed at any earlier stage, themselves, have questions of you. You are testifying under an expedited procedure which the Tribunal has -- And if I may interrupt myself briefly to ask Defence counsel whether they have an indication and to how much time they expect that they would spend in cross-examination, because I don't have an update on what is before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we announced three hours for this witness before, but I believe one session will be sufficient because of your decision in which you gave written reasons when you admitted the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if there's anything after my learned friend Mr. Krgovic, I will ask the question some witnesses [as interpreted]. But, in essence, I have no questions planned for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Mr. Witness, and we would refer to you as Mr. Witness because of the protective measures which you have been afforded, you would have heard from what has passed between the Bench and Defence counsel as to how long they expect that they would spend in cross-examination. The Prosecution will spend 45 minutes in their examination-in-chief, so the net result is that your testimony would be completed within the compass of today's sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we are back. And, Mr. Witness, continuing where we were before the technical difficulties required us to pause, you would have heard from what has passed between the Bench and Defence counsel that they expect that the -- of the time that they expect to spend with you, and the Prosecution has 45 minutes for their questions, so the result is that your testimony is expected to be completed before the Court rises today. And I would now invite counsel for the Prosecution to begin their questions. And I expect that in terms of such preliminary matters as he has, we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Your Honours, because I'm just going to ask the standard 92 ter questions. And his prior testimony wasn't in closed sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I first want to ask a few questions regarding your prior testimony before this Tribunal. Did you testify in the Brdjanin case in April 2002?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Prior to testifying here today, did you have the opportunity to listen to an audio recording of your prior testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And was that recording an accurate reflection of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In the 45 minutes I have with you, I just want to clarify some of the matters that you testified about in your prior testimony. In the Brdjanin case, you testified about police officers in blue camouflage uniforms who drove around Banja Luka in 1992 in a red van, or a red kombi, terrorising the non-Serb population. And you mentioned that Bosko Vuksan was consistently among these police officers. Sir, besides Vuksan, were the other police officers in the red kombi always the same?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Vuksan was there the most frequently. However, they would come as a squad of seven to ten men, and they weren't always the same men.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You testified previously that the red kombi began operating in the spring of 1992 and that you had a personal encounter with this van in winter of 1992. Could you tell us, for how long did this red kombi operate in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: At the beginning, they had other vehicles as well. As far as I recall, the red kombi was there in 1992 and 1993, when I left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when did you leave Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: In November of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Focussing on 1992, would you see this red kombi parked at any of the government buildings in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: It was a police vehicle, so they were under the jurisdiction of the Banja Luka SUP. You could often see them at the leather and fur factory in the Deovici. And towards the end, they were most frequently at the old army centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would you see it, this red kombi, parked outside the CSB building?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We object to that. I mean, it's leading, isn't it? The witness clearly said when he saw this kombi. What is the point of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't believe it's leading, Your Honours. I'm just asking him whether he saw it in -- at the CSB building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, did you see this red kombi parked at the CSB building in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, in your prior testimony, you mention that check-points were established throughout Banja Luka. Can you tell us when these check-points were first established?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: The check-points that I had to go through were established in April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who manned these check-points?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: They were manned by reservists, by police reservists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in order to pass through these check-points, did non-Serbs have to have certain documentation?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: At that time, they required us to have passes. And anybody who didn't have such a pass, couldn't get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were Serbs required to have these passes?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I am not sure. I believe they checked everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If a non-Serb had one of these passes or had proper documentation, were they always allowed to pass through these check-points, or sometimes they were not allowed to pass through them?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: If you didn't have the appropriate document, that is, the pass for movement, you couldn't get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you didn't understand my question. My question is: Non-Serbs who did have proper documentation, were they, nonetheless, prevented from getting through these check-points, on occasions?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I understand you now. There were such cases. They were very insolent anyway. And if one of us showed a pass, they would take it and simply tear it up and say, Well, you no longer have it now. There were many such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what impact did these check-points have on the ability of non-Serbs to move around Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to describe the situation that prevailed at the time. But if you are confined in a very small area without any possibility of movement to do your everyday business and shopping and things like that, a man feels as if he were in a ghetto, as if he were an inferior person. And that had a great impact on all the people, because that was psychologically very detrimental. We felt like second-class citizens or enemies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just one further question regarding this documentation that non-Serbs had to obtain to even get through these check-points. Was this documentation difficult for non-Serbs to get at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes. Initially, we were able to get a pass or two at the local commune. Later on, these passes were issued by the military draft office. For those who had work obligation, the passes were probably issued to them by their units. But, generally speaking, it was very difficult to obtain one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also testified previously about the resettlement agencies that were established in Banja Luka in 1992. And, in fact, your daughter used one of these agencies in September of 1992. Can you tell us, if a non-Serb wanted to leave Banja Luka, did they have to use one of these agencies?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: We all had to take this route, because that was the only route to take. These agencies appeared and provided and organised bus transportation to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In order to use one of these agencies, did non-Serbs have to pay a fee to the agency?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: If you allow me, I would like just to say that even if you are to come to the point where you can use the services of this agency, you had to do a lot of things ahead of that, including payments. For example, one had to prepare all the certificates confirming that all the utility bills had been paid. You also had to have a certificate from a bank confirming that you are not in the red. Then you had to register with -- or, rather, de-register from the draft office and then register with the SUP. After you have collected all these papers, in the neighbourhood of Mejdan there was a prefabricated building where you get -- you -- the resettlement people, and then you had to join the queue, because there were hundreds, if not thousands, of people who were waiting to get out. So that was the route and the procedure for getting out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned that they -- that the non-Serbs who wanted to leave Banja Luka had to pay various fees to municipal organs; but did they also have to pay a fee to these agencies themselves, to be transported out of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: In order for one to get the document that we referred to as resettlement paper, a cheque had to be filled. I cannot tell you in which amount because I don't remember. But after you have done that, you have to sign the resettlement paper confirming that you concede to leave all your mobile and immobile property to be disposed of by Republika Srpska. Only after the payment has been effected and after one has collected all the papers that I mentioned earlier, then you take the resettlement paper as the main document, you go to the agency, and they provide transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now with regard to these -- this transportation, did these buses have escorts?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who --

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: The police secured the transportation. And I can speak about the first organisation, or company. I don't know. It was owned by a woman called Perka. She was the one who notified the people who were interested about the schedule of departure. She determined the schedule of buses. There were, daily, some dozen buses of hers leaving, but sometimes she had -- had to -- to postpone the departures because she was constantly in negotiations with the Croats, who had to give their approval. So this is how people left for Croatia, in these convoys, of course, with proper security and escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did the police escorts conduct any searches of the non-Serbs on these buses?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: The main search was conducted either before or at the Bosanska Gradiska border crossings. This is where the Serb policemen conducted a thorough search, partly of the buses, or on the buses. Which was followed by their taking all the people outside, where there were containers, so to speak, where they conducted another detailed search. These Serb policemen took away all the valuables. They simply seized items of gold, money, everything they fancied. They even established the limit of the money that one can carry with -- with them. If I'm not wrong, I think that this limit was 300 German marks. And with this kind of restrictions, I believe that this offered an excellent opportunity for looting and seizing everything that they liked. In addition to that, they used an extremely abusive language. We were humiliated. We were ill-treated. Which is difficult to comprehend. I mean, the extent to which a human being can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to move to a different topic now. In your prior testimony, you described how two police inspectors took you to the SUP in summer 1992, where they and a Drago Samardzija interrogated and beat you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can we have P35 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, what we have in front of us is a photograph. Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: That's the Banja Luka SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, is this where you were interrogated and beaten on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what floor you were on when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I think -- I think that I was on the second floor. When you enter the building, you go a couple of metres ahead, and on the left-hand side was Mr. Samardzija's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And can you tell us approximately what time of day this interrogation took place?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I think it started at around 10.00. I forgot to mention that on the other side of this building was the office where I was brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, again, that was on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And you said your interrogation started around 10.00. Was that in the morning or at night?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: In the morning. In the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You mentioned in your prior testimony that you knew Samardzija from before the conflict. What position did he hold before the war?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: He also worked at the SUP. And, as far as I know, he was an officer or a clerk for materiel procurement and assets. I think that's how we would call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you know what position he held in 1992, once the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I don't know, because, probably, changes took place. Hence, I don't know which post he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In your prior testimony, you go into considerable detail regarding your interrogation and beating, so I won't ask you to repeat that today. But can you tell us what happened after the three police officers had finished beating you?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for sparing me the request for recounting the details of probably one of the worst days in my life. When these men took me out of the office, they threatened me in the most strict -- in the strictest terms, not to mention anything about this to anyone. If I would not comply with that, that would mean the end of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Having said that, was your experience at the CSB building unique, or do you know about other non-Serbs who suffered similar treatment at the CSB building in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how this question can be fitted in with the adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, the adjudicated fact deals with campaigns of intimidation, perilous living conditions. The Trial Chamber has admitted this witness's testimony regarding his own beatings. I thin it is relevant, whether he heard about other such incidents from other non-Serbs that he knew in the community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question? Did you know about other non-Serbs who had received similar treatment at the CSB building in 1992, as you did?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I definitely do know that, because a huge number of people were involved. I can give you the names of the people for whom I know for sure that were severely beaten in this particular building. It was no secret among our people. Everybody knew that that was common practice. So I can fully ascertain that in this building there were quite a few beatings and interrogations, the purpose of which was to seek something that, in my mind, was completely pointless and devoid of any purpose. The most frequent reason for that was to get hold of material belongings, as was in my case, or to intimidate the people. That was their aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, during your prior testimony, when you were asked to describe life in Banja Luka for the non-Serb population in 1992, you stated that there were shootings and killings. Can you provide us with a little more detail about those crimes? Who were the perpetrators and who were the victims?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: One cannot have enough words to describe the situation of non-Serbs in Banja Luka in 1992. A minute ago I spoke about the restriction of movement imposed on us. We were under constant surveillance. People who were going to or back from the front line would resort to senseless shooting at the buildings and places of shrine -- of -- of worship. Believe me, I can tell you that in my neighbourhood where the road ends, we could collect piles of casings from the bullets fired by the Serb soldiers. One such incident of the shooting at the buildings and houses resulted in a death and also another person was seriously wounded. Do you want me to tell you the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That won't be necessary at this stage. And I think it's included in your prior testimony. But, can you tell us, just to clarifies, these homes, businesses, and shrines that were being targeted, were they non-Serb property?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, nearly 100 per cent of the residents were Muslims. There were a few houses - how shall I put it? - with mixed marriages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: From what you could observe, were these random acts of violence, or did they appear to be organised to you?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: That was almost a rule. For example, if they see a mosque, and there were four of them in my neighbourhood, they just couldn't help passing by without opening fire. That was a rule. Those were visible signs of what they did. You could see bullet-holes. As soon as the shooting would start, people would scatter around as far from the main street as possible and seek shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was your own business targeted?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: The building where I lived was damaged, and the wall next to the building was targeted and hit by a mortar shell. People came to see it, and I showed this to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's what I want to move on to at this point. From what you were able to observe in 1992, were the police doing anything to prevent these kind of crimes from being committed against the non-Serb population in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I think that they did quite the contrary. In 1992, we had meetings with representatives of the civilian, military, and police authorities in Banja Luka because we had complaints about the situation which we felt was unbearable. However, I have a feeling that this meeting was completely counter-productive, and that after that, we were subjected to even greater torture. They assigned patrols for the neighbourhood in which I lived. We thought that that would be a relief. However, the situation worsened. All these people who were there to protect us, their -- they would seize money from people via their informers and they also collected information in order to be able to take people to the police headquarters, to interrogate them and intimidate them. And I can confirm that there was absolutely no reason for that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify, who was performing these patrols in the Muslim neighbourhoods?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: The Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a meeting in 1992. Did you attend a meeting in Gornji Seher in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I would just like to go back a little. Before that meeting in August at the swimming pool owned by Dzemil Kobilj, a meeting was held at the local commune, which was also attended by the civilian, military, and police authorities. Now back to your question. Yes, in August of 1992, I attended the meeting at the swimming pool. Mr. Predrag Radic, the mayor, was there; Mr. Stojan Zupljanin, the chief of SUP was there; and there was a military person, I think his rank was major, and his last name was Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us were there -- who were the Muslim representatives at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: This meeting was attended by representatives of the Muslims who were rather influential within their community, who had certain authority. But I would like to add that apart from the Muslims, there were 80 of us, because each neighbourhood sent two representatives. And I think that there was some 30-odd Serbs there as well. Maybe less; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall, was Dzevad Osmancevic there?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember him being present. This meeting had been initiated by Mr. Adem Gunic, an engineer who was, at the time, the deputy mayor; then Sadik Beglerovic and Dzevad Osmancevic. As far as I know, those three people asked the gentlemen that I mentioned - Radic, Zupljanin, and Ilic - to come and to address our people, because they wished for a joint solution to be found in order to suppress such phenomena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, let me just remind you that you have about eight minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what information -- at this meeting, what information did the Muslim representatives provide to the Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: We informed them thoroughly about all forms of provocations, the ceaseless firing, shooting, incursions onto private property, ban on movements. Because, despite the ban on movement during the night, there was also a curfew from 9.00 in the evening to 6.00 in the morning, during which time you were not allowed out on the streets. Nobody dared leave their yard. So that we simply asked those present to find a solution to reduce the shooting, to maintain some kind of control. And the result of the meeting were these patrols that they introduced, which also didn't prove to be that great, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was the red kombi brought up at this meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I don't remember the kombi at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I mean -- let me rephrase my question. Was -- did the Muslim representatives tell the Serb representatives about the red kombi incidents at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Absolutely. I think that the worst thing that happened in Banja Luka was precisely that kombi that everybody feared, and we asked that something be done so that those people would be stopped, prevented from sowing fear all over Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were the Serb representatives surprised by all this information provided by the Muslim representatives?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: All I can say is that everyone promised to do everything in their power to improve the situation, and I think that they were not surprised, because the people who initiated the meeting had to have -- inform them about what was going on in our area so that they knew that they were coming to the meeting because of problems that we had mentioned earlier. So they were not surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But was there any suggestion that the non-Serbs were creating these problems for themselves?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: One of those present said that the Muslim population, which was the majority population there, were not looking at the situation realistically, that they had to understand that it was war, and that they had to respond to the call-up in as a greater number as possible. And everything that was mentioned, he kind of implied that we, ourselves, were responsible for that situation. I have to point out, though, that the gentlemen did promise that they would do everything in their power to improve the situation. If I may add something. Things turned out quite differently. The next day already, there were raids - that's what we called them - on a wide scale. And only -- alone in the Sitari settlement they searched several hundred houses, brought in scores of people. They spread fear everywhere. And in the area where I was, with the appearance of these policemen, things became even worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that's why I want to clarify: Who conducted these raids?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: The Serbian police. They did the searches with the most frequent explanation, that they were looking for weapons, that they were looking for those who didn't respond to the call-up, to bring them in. And let me just say this, too: They looted and took everything that they liked. If they couldn't take something that they liked right away, they would order that this be set aside for them because they were going to come the next day or at some other time, that they had determined to pick up those things. With the instruction that the homeowner, the host, shouldn't tell anybody anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just -- my final question is a clarification. These searches and arrests against -- who were they against? Were they against non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Mostly against non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to make a clarification on the record. The previous pseudonym sheet of Witness ST-223 should be Exhibit P01743 and not P01742 as previously indicated. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I am Dragan Krgovic, representing Mr. Zupljanin. I'm going to be putting some questions to you regarding your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Go ahead please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: First one clarification. You spoke about the procedure during border crossing, when people from these different organisations would cross. These convoys, actually. You did not leave with that convoy in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think that were following. I said, loud and clear, that I left on the 15th of November, 1993. So I don't see actually why you're putting this question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see what you testified about today about searches at the border and the confiscation of items. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is reliable, definite data, because I saw that, myself, in 1993. People who went through this were members of my own family. My wife, my daughter, my son, and my daughter in law.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My question was that in 1992 you personally did not see these things. You can just answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I think this is a ridiculous question, and I'm repeating that I left in 1993. So how could I also leave in 1992 then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But this is why I'm asking you this. Precisely. You did not see, personally, these things that you are testifying about. Can you please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I did see them in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see them in 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you have an intervention?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, just that the interpreter said that she was unable to complete the witness's prior answer about members of his family leaving through these convoys in 1992. And, I don't know, it's probably too late now to go back to that question, but we've missed part of his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. I would remind the witness and counsel to remember that the evidence has to be interpreted. So, Mr. Witness, please wait for counsel to complete his question before you begin to answer. And counsel, of course, you would wait for the answer before you proceed to your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps if you can answer once again. In 1992, you personally were not at the Gradiska border crossing. Isn't that right? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So what you testified about in response to Mr. Olmsted's question is something that you heard from others; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to 1992, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You also responded to the Prosecutor's questions about the black [as interpreted] kombi that was parked. And you mentioned a couple of locations in your earlier statements. You said that you never saw this vehicle in front of the CSB.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Red kombi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krgovic, were you in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I just want to tell you one thing. There was no place in town where at some point the red kombi was not parked. You need to know that. It was either in front of the SUP or in front of the old army hall, in front of the daumic [phoen], in front of the Boska. The kombi could be seen in any part of town. I am telling you this for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your previous testimony you didn't mention that you saw this vehicle in front of the CSB. You mentioned the JNA hall, the Mali Logor camp. You mentioned the barracks where the 4th Infantry Brigade was located. But you never mentioned that you saw it in front of the CSB. Is that correct? That is the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Do you think that after so many years a person can remember all the locations? That perhaps he is not permitted to skip a location which simply doesn't occur to one at that point? I think it would have been better if you had asked me whether this was true or not. And I'm telling you it is 100 per cent true, what I'm telling. If I happen to forget something, if I don't recall a date, please don't hold it against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you allow for the possibility that in your previous testimony you never mentioned that you saw the red kombi parked in front of the CSB; isn't that right? And I am telling you that I looked at all of your statement and I never found a references to that.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: As far as I can remember my testimony, I think that I did not mention the CSB. But that does not mean that what I'm saying today is not true. This is 100 per cent true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you talked about documents that were necessary in order to be able to leave Banja Luka, you mentioned a certificate where one would have to leave all movable and immovable property to the Serbian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign something like that?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I couldn't have a copy of it. You would hand that in. The document was called a resettlement paper. Nobody could leave without the resettlement paper. And if you want, I will say it again: In order for a person to leave, he had to pay all his bills, the rent, electricity, garbage, other utilities, any other bills. He had to provide a letter from the bank that he was not in debt, that he didn't owe anything to the state. He needed to bring a certificate from the SUP, a certificate from the military department, then go and make a payment in the bank - I don't remember which amount exactly - and then the resettlement paper, which was a thicker piece of paper, literally stated that the signee renounced or gave up all of his movable and immovable property in favour of Republika Srpska. Only when you received the resettlement paper where you would spend hours in line next to the city bridge on the left bank of the Vrbas -- no, actually, on the right bank of the Vrbas, on the left-hand side opposite the Vrbas river, next to the Kastel, was the local commune where these resettlement papers were issued. That was the only way for us to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you never left your property to Republika Srpska, as a matter of fact; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I don't know whom I left it to. At the time, it was called Krajina or Republika Srpska. In any case, it was the state. This was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you sold that property later; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: No, never. Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you still have that property that you allegedly gave to Republika Srpska? You are still the owner of that property, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to refrain from provocative questions. I didn't allegedly hand it over. I really had to sign this. Not just me, but every single citizen who was leaving. This is the truth. You cannot evade that. Everyone knows that. It's not just me. And the conditions under which I had to do that are known. The conditions in which a person would sign such an agreement are known. These are conditions when you do not have any other way. You have no possible choice. You just are focussed on saving your life. That -- that is when property is of no consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, you are still the owner of the property for which you claim that you handed over to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you were speaking about this meeting in Gornji Seher, Mr. Tutus, the chief of the Banja Luka Public Security Station, did he attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I seem to recollect that Predrag Radic was there, Mr. Zupljanin; and I said, if I remember correctly, there was a major from the military. He was definitely from the military. And his name was Ilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I don't know if you've left this question of the property, but I have a -- there's a clarifying question I wish to put to the witness. Mr. Witness, you -- in response to counsel's question, as to whether you were still the owner of the property for which you claim you handed over to Republika Srpska, you answered affirmatively. Are you in possession of this property, the property of which counsel spoke, to the extent that you understood his question? Or -- could you expand on your answer for me, please. I don't want to put words in your mouth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said that in order for a person to be able to leave Banja Luka, he had to sign a document which was called the resettlement paper and which, without any doubt, clearly stated that by leaving, a person was leaving behind all of their movable and immovable property to the state. However, after all these events were over, our expulsion, in 2002, I again got my property back, and now it is in my possession again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Mr. Krgovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I would like ... oh, no, sorry, I misunderstood. It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And to stick with the question His Honour Judge Hall put to you, there were no changes to the title deed of -- of your property. There was no transfer from you to the state. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: All the property is 100 per cent in my name. I am the full owner. As for who used, managed, or had the property in their hands for a while, I don't know. But today, the property is in my name, just as it was before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as far as you know, there was no change in the land property register?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krgovic, please, what is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this question put by my learned friend Mr. Olmsted during the examination-in-chief, that he had to hand his property over to the state in order to be able to leave, I am trying to show that this practically never happened. This is why I'm asking if there were any changes in the land register. Was the ownership transferred to the state, to Republika Srpska, and then transferred back to him again. This is what I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I don't quite understand. Are you challenging the testimony that he got it back in 2002, which means that between 1992 and 2002 he didn't have it? Or at least -- or at least he thought he didn't have it because he handed it over to -- are you challenging the handing over?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We're talking about a change in ownership here, because the testimony of the witness was that he had to sign over the property to Republika Srpska. These are two things: Possession and ownership. These are two different categories. The ownership and possession. I think that it was his testimony that he had to transfer ownership to Republika Srpska, if I understood him correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I give an explanation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And -- and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is that this is not correct. It is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And were people told so at the -- at the moment they handed over what they thought to be their property and what you say was their possession? Were they told so, that it was only the possession that they handed over, and not the ownership?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this could be clearly seen if there was such a certificate. That's why I asked him. But we did not find any such certificate, at least as far as Banja Luka is concerned. We didn't find it. There are similar certificates in other municipalities, but I have not seen anything of that kind that the witness was talking about. Perhaps the Prosecutor would gladly have that, and they would tender that happily, if they were in possession of such a certificate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the lawyer of the gentleman knows full well, even if he never had a resettlement paper in his hand, the resettlement paper clearly states, and this is something that nobody can deny or doubt in any way, and that confirms that on the basis of the resettlement paper, I agreed to hand over my property to the state. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) so that there is no confusion and what I said cannot be put into doubt. There is also my request for restitution of property and a ruling in my favour, and all of that indicates that I am telling the full truth, just as I said right at the beginning when I was standing at this witness-stand. You cannot doubt this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's time for a break now. Perhaps it's a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just out of an abundance caution, I think that the part about the details of the people taking over the witness's house have to be redacted. Somewhere in 28, line 10 to 17. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the break and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, just one moment, please. Mr. Witness -- oh, I'll just wait. Mr. Witness, the moment you signed over your -- your house, or your houses, to the state, did -- did you think that that was handing over forever, or just for the time of you being away? Or something else? Was it handing over the entire property for good? Or was it something else? Was it just temporarily? In your understanding, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to give a broader reply to this question, if you'll allow me. My assessment of the war was false from the very beginning, because I thought that all of that would blow over quickly, that it would end, and that I personally was not guilty of anything. I did not owe anybody anything. And that, for that reason, I might be spared of any kind of problems. At the beginning, I must admit that I felt sorry to leave everything that I had gained by working, because everything that I gained, I gained by working. The example that I sent my child away from Banja Luka when she was 15 confirms this, as does the fact that I sent my wife, my son, my sister-in-law, and my grandchild away and stayed in the house alone. However, as the situation became increasingly complex and as the problems increased from day to day - and let me emphasise that it was with the help of an international organisation of the UNHCR - I was taken out of Banja Luka to Zagreb. I never thought that I would leave my property behind. I never intended that. But that was the only way to leave. That was the only possibility for leaving Banja Luka. I realized that I had to agree to relinquishing my property. Deep down, I still had hope that I would return to my home, but I was fully aware that I had lost everything that I had. I didn't think that there was a way for me to return and that all this would be mine once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And how, then, did you recover your property, as you said, in 2002?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know when exactly, but an office for the restitution of property was established in Banja Luka. They were housed in pre-fabricated houses near the town clinic. Our people would go there, as did I, from all over Europe, even the United States, and they filed requests for the restitution of property. Allegedly, before then, the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Petric, had passed a decision that all the property had to be returned to their previous owners. Relying on that decision, I also applied for the restitution of my property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, as it says in the statement, you didn't go to the court to have it certified that you were relinquishing your property in favour of Republika Srpska; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I didn't mention a court. I said that apart from the certificates and the report made with the SUP and the military department, you would receive this certificate on the right bank of the Vrbas river, near the local commune, and it was called the resettlement paper. If that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what you later said about people who stayed in your houses, these were refugees, Serbian refugees, who had had come from Kljuc to Banja Luka and were assigned these houses for temporary use; they were allowed to use your immovables temporarily?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I said that loud and clear. They received decisions allowing them to stay in my houses. They were given decisions. They were allowed to use my houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you filed a request to -- for the restitution of your property, they agreed to move out and to hand your property back to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: We were called to the premises that I mentioned earlier, at the clinic, together. And there, in the presence of an official, we agreed on the terms, agreed when they were supposed to leave and when I was to take over my property. These were so-called evictions, and they were done with the help of the police in order to avoid any problematic situations. Because usually during the handover one of the parties, usually the person living there, refused to leave. So evictions were organised. There were forced evictions and all kinds of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you also talked about some events, attacks on Muslim and Croat civilians. Did you know that the police in Banja Luka arrested and escorted into custody people who attacked Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I must admit that I had limited information about this, but I know that they had to take certain measures and certain activities because the situation in Banja Luka was hopeless. There was terror, looting, murders, and I believe that the police had to take measures against such cases. I don't know about individual cases personally, but I believe, as a person, that they had to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that among those arrested who were suspected of attacking Muslims and Croats in Banja Luka in 1992, there were some people who used the red kombi in order to terrorise and instill fear among the Muslim and Croat population?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I don't know. As for the red kombi that I am talking about, I think it was neither borrowed, nor could it have been used by anybody other than the police that I talked about. And let me tell you this: Bosko Vuksan worked at the shoe factory in Banja Luka, and his brother was one of my bosses. Zuco, as we called him, is a private entrepreneur from Rudarska. He -- he made tombstones. We were good friends. We hunted together. So the people who were in this red van were people that we knew. We knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you, you talked about some shootings and murders that took place in Banja Luka, and you said you were an eye-witness to some of them. Did you know that the military police or the police arrested a person who killed two Muslims? I'm talking about Avdo Softic and the other man. You know the other name better than I do. It was in your neighbourhood. Right?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I will correct you about the last name. His last name was not "Softic"; it was "Sofic." It does not have a T. And his first name is Avdo. The second man was Ramiz Zdenac. They were killed in the centre of our settlement on the old road on the 5th of December, 1992. They were killed by Zeljko Ceko, a young man who lived very close to our settlement. As far as I know, I was informed that he was taken into custody. He was in detention for a while. Apparently he was under investigation, because it's a remand prison, as far as I know. You surely know what I mean. But I know that for such a crime, he was never convicted; at least not while I was there. His punishment was that he was sent to the front line. Whether he was later convicted, for how long, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you happen to know the profession of this gentleman, Mr. Zeljko Ceko? What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe he was a labourer. His father worked at the market. I don't know his exact occupation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you know that after these two men were killed, the police cordoned off the entire area in search of the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And soon after, he was arrested and taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 2D03-1340.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, while this is being pulled up, I should just note that in the Trial Chamber's decision they issued last night, his testimony concerning this particular case was excluded from his 92 ter package. I'm wondering whether, in light of Defence counsel's persistence in this particular case, this case of a killing, that that decision should be amended to include his testimony with regard to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond to this. The reason I'm showing this document is that the Prosecution, in its examination-in-chief, expanded the testimony of this witness in relation to the statement and asked what the police and other organs did in order to take measures against the perpetrators of certain crimes committed against Muslim and Croats. The witness replied that he didn't know. And to my question he said that he didn't know about this. So I want to show him this document in relation to what the witness said in the examination-in-chief so we could identify the person he talked about and whether he belonged to any institution, as Judge Harhoff asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. If I may say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment -- just a moment, please, while resolve this objection that's taken by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We agree with the objection taken by Mr. Olmsted. This -- putting this particular document falls outside of the specific adjudicated fact to which this witness was called to testify. And that although Mr. Olmsted was permitted to ask a general question, to which, as I recall, there was an objection which was overruled, we do not think that that general question is sufficiently -- was sufficient to open the way to deal with specific questions raised in this document because then that would -- the Chamber would -- would, in effect, be reversing a ruling it's already given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your examination-in-chief, you mentioned an incident when a wall next to your house was hit by a missile from a hand-held rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you reported that to the police. The police visited the scene and carried out an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: That's correct. It was done by the patrol which was patrolling our neighbourhood. Their response was that that was something normal, only to be expected, and that we were lucky not to have sustained any injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Banja Luka Police actually arrested a group of people involved in such attacks where rocket-launchers were used?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I said at the beginning that our movement was restricted. We virtually lived in a ghetto. We were not allowed to move around. I was fond of reading newspapers, but since it was difficult to get, buy, them, I sometimes asked the people who went to town to procure them for me. I also obtained some information on the radio and on TV. But in spite of that, we didn't have a clear picture of the situation. And nobody actually asked what the police was doing. That's not the case nowadays. Everybody knows what the police work involves, that is, preserving law and order and things of that nature. Therefore, it was beyond my realm of interest to ask whether the police were arresting someone and what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned your visit to the police headquarters. Sir, isn't it true that that the police summoned you on account of suspicions that you were involved in some illegal activities, that you were a member of the so-called Walter Group which was organised by the SDA Banja Luka and that it was involved in intelligence operations?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I never went to the police for those reasons, and I was never questioned or interrogated about these issues. The only reason that they arrested me was to beat me, to humiliate me, and do other things. I only heard about this group that you are mentioning after the war, when some people were arrested, like Smail Djuzel; his wife, Suhreta; and another man from Pobrdje. I don't know who else was convicted. However, as far as I'm concerned, I never heard a word about this until I left Banja Luka. I had never been brought in by the police for those reasons, and this group was never mentioned. Only after the war did I learn that I been sentenced to 12 years in prison, purportedly for treason and intelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that alongside Mr. Korzic [phoen] and the other individuals you just mentioned, you organised collection and delivery of military intelligence or the information pertaining to the situation in Banja Luka and that you sent this information to the Embassy of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zagreb and other foreign missions?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Sir, I think that are you wasting your time. A while ago I reiterated twice that my movements were restricted, that I never ventured out, that I did not meet any people, and that I heard about this organisation called Walter only after the war. Nobody ever asked me a single question about this, nor did they accuse me of this kind of activities. Therefore, I'm asking you, what kind of information, intelligence, could I have conveyed to Zagreb, bearing in mind that I was living in the part of town where there was no electricity, where there was curfew, where there was limited movement, et cetera? I really don't understand where you got this from. Who told you that I could have done such things, given that it is well known that after 9.00 in the evening I couldn't even leave my yard and during the daylight I could only go outside into the streets? So this is a total fabrication. And it is additionally confirmed by the fact that when I returned to Banja Luka, to this date, nobody ever asked me anything about this. They never called me into account, and, God forbid, I never served the sentence that you are mentioning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that you wrote a report, or reports, in which you described the position of Croats and Muslims in Banja Luka as being actually worse than it actually was and that women and children were being killed in the area of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, what would be the dates of the period of these reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, this is a blatant lie. Tell me, first, to whom could I have sent a report of that kind? You are talking about thousands of dead people. What are you talking about? You see that this is completely groundless. And if you claim that it was I who sent those reports, could you be so kind at least to show me a portion of such report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Witness, counsel is, in the course of cross-examination, putting his case, and he is doing his job. If he asks an improper question, the Chamber would certainly intervene. But it would speed matters along if you would listen carefully to counsel's question and then answer as simply and clearly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the witness said you are talking about thousands of dead people. Did you mention that? because in the -- in the transcript, in your question, I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, maybe it wasn't recorded. I talked about tens of thousands of women and children killed in the area of Prijedor and Krajina, that the witness reported about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reported about this? No. Never, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). And I said at the very beginning that I never sent a word to anyone, nor did I provide any information to anyone, nor was I involved in that kind of activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And to clarify this matter, there is a document in the list of the Prosecution's exhibits for this witness which I believe Mr. Krgovic is referring to, and as the witness has testified, it does not -- he was not the author of that document. And, therefore, I would was going to object, but the witness obviously picked up on the issue himself and corrected Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not talking about this specific document. I am talking about the whole series of documents from which this question generates, and I intend to show them to the witness. I'm not talking about this document, and my questions do not relate to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that together with Mr. Kjazim Durakovic you organised and attended the meetings in which you gathered information about the developments in Banja Luka, and that you assisted Mr. Krzic while he was in Banja Luka, as well, Mithad Smajic, Amir Novalija, and Osman Gujacic, in the activities of this kind?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: You're going back again to what I deny and have denied from the very beginning. I can confirm that I had no links whatsoever with that organisation. I believe that you all know that this was all a fabrication. And I really don't know where this idea came from about my being in co-operation with Kjazim Durakovic, who had never been an activist throughout his life. He never did anything, except, perhaps, being active in the trade union. As I said, with regard to these activities, this could only be made up in order to exert pressure on our people to leave Banja Luka, to expel them. And as for espionage and activities of that sort, particularly when it comes to the people from my neighbourhood, I can tell you again that there is nothing to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you had a code-name, Ivo, in that group, and that is how the other members of the group addressed you?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: If you permit me, you are making me say things that have no sense. From the very first word on, I deny, I've been trying to prove, and I'm stating that I have nothing to do whatsoever with the group in question. Had I had anything to do with it, members of the police, or whoever is in charge of that, would have brought -- taken me in and interrogated me and would have taken certain measures. And I repeat: If we're talking about the authorities, civilian, military, police authorities, I never discussed any illegal [Realtime transcript read in error "legal"] activities of mine with them, and I never did anything in relation to reports of this kind. The most weird thing would be that I had a pseudonym, a code-name, that being Ivo. That is very, very far from the truth. That makes no sense whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just an intervention in the transcript. I believe page 37, line 21, I believe the witness said: I never discussed any "illegal" activities. Not "legal" activities. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you are probably aware that this group of people that I mentioned, this group Walter, was brought to trial in Banja Luka, some of them. And before the indictments were issued, some of them provided statements in the SUP and to the investigating judge, and that is where they mentioned your name. Are aware of this fact and of these details that I just asked you about?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: As for them giving statements and who they gave them to, that's something I don't know. But I am stating, once again, that that has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness look at 2D03-1521 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I question whether this is going beyond simply trying to challenge this witness's credibility. This is with regard to allegations of a spy network, where this witness has clearly stated that he had nothing to do with. He acknowledged that at some point charges were filed against him but they were baseless and he was not even in the country at the time. So how does this hinge on his credibility at this stage, and how does this even relate to the adjudicated fact which is at issue for this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was asking the witness about these facts, and I put it to him clearly that this was the reason for his arrest. And now I'm showing documents to him that confirm this, because it is the position of the Prosecution that these people were brought in only because they were Muslims and so forth, for no other reason; and I'm trying to prove the very opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In want to show the witness these documents which show the reason for this whole series of questions that I put to him. The document and the questions have direct relevance to the testimony of this witness in terms of Rule 92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would have thought, though, Mr. Krgovic, that having put the question directly to the witness and having received an answer, that's it, as far as this witness is concerned. But give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at this document. You've had the opportunity to read the contents of the document on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It can be concluded, on the basis of this document, when asked about you specifically, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want to mention his name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please take into account that we don't have an English translation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm just going to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you agree that this is an Official Note from the 15th of September, 1994, given by this person that you know? Do you know Smail Djuzel?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I will tell you. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, just answer my question, please. Do you know Smail Djuzel?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: I have to give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can give an explanation when the Prosecutor asks you. I don't have too much time for my cross-examination. I want to cover this quickly.

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Smail Djuzel, and I know Muharem Krzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... were under the impression that the document you wanted to show was a document dating from the time the witness was still living in Banja Luka, in 1992/1993. This is obviously something from a later date. 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But it speaks about the events. It speaks about the witness specifically. And events when the witness was living in Banja Luka in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So it's -- it's not an Official Note because that was -- that was the basis on -- on -- on which we accepted this ... this is not -- this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an Official Note, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this is not an Official Note of the interrogation of the witness, when he was brought to the police building in Banja Luka while still living in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. This is an Official Note on the basis of which an indictment was issued and a ruling was issued that the witness referred to. I can show the judgement, the ruling, to the witness. I can show him the basis on which there was suspicion that the witness took part in certain activities. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... but then this --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but let me say, this is the initial -- the starting document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But then this is -- this is an Official Note. Is this an Official -- this is an Official Note. This is not a witness -- this is not a statement of the witness. Or is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, this is not a statement by the witness. It's not anyone's statement. This is an Official Note made by a MUP member who was investigating the activities of this Walter Group and the activities of the witness, among other things. It was made in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I happen to have an English translation of this document, and it doesn't relate to events in 1992. And, in fact, the only portion which mentions this witness talks about after this witness left the Republika Srpska, which, as this witness has testified, was in November of 1993. I just wanted to correct that. And, otherwise, it is an Official Note by a person who is not a party and who is not present before this Tribunal to testify regarding the truth of the matters asserted in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we misunderstood the -- what this document would have contained. And it is now the view of the Chamber that it is an irrelevant issue, so please move on to something else. It's entirely collateral to the issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one question. Is it the position of the Prosecutor that the Official Note taken from a person who did not testify before the Tribunal should not be part of the documents in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Our position, Your Honours, is this -- this statement was taken in 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Olmsted --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Krgovic, the Trial Chamber's decision has nothing to do with -- with the OTP's position on Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I understand. [Interpretation] Could we then show the witness 2D03-1453.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that you heard that you were convicted and sentenced to a prison term of 12 years, actually, 13 years' imprisonment, for espionage. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Yes. I said today, also, that I was informed after the war only that for alleged membership of this group I had been sentenced to 12 years in prison for espionage. This is the information that I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have the opportunity to look at the judgement according to which you were sentenced?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly like to move to private session. And can we redact this part of the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe for the record, I would like to mention that we started in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the reference I made in the transcript, it's on page 18 in the Serbian version, when I spoke about a verdict being handed down in absentia. So can we please have page 18, and page 16 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Should we revert --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked for this document not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we should revert to private session, Mr. Krgovic, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just for reference, I'm just going to show this portion that Judge Harhoff's question referred to. One can see clearly what is this all about in the last paragraph in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I accept that, Mr. Krgovic. And I -- but I already did take your word for it. Obviously these people were tried in absentia, and that's fine. But, still, I - speaking for myself, at least - I'm not convinced that this witness is the person who is mentioned in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we just move into private session for my next question, to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic. Yes, Mr. Olmsted, anything in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 10216 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what we're looking at is the ARK Crisis Staff Official Gazette dated 23 June 1992. And I would like you to look at, in particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
