utterances.text: If we turn to page 13 of the English, page 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I want, sir, to focus your attention to this decision that's numbered number 45. Under which it states: "The proper municipal organs of administration shall be informed of all abandoned property, which shall then be proclaimed property of the state and placed at the disposal of municipal assemblies." Sir, how did this language in this decision compare to the waiver that you had to sign?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I did not show this document to the witness. And, second of all, this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's not a leading question, Your Honours. In fact, I kind of wish that Defence counsel did show this document to the witness. And I'm showing it to him now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you should first ask him whether he is familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's not the point of my question. I'm asking the witness to compare the waiver that he had to sign in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this decision that's in front of you, regarding property being proclaimed property of the state and placed at the disposal of the municipal assemblies, how did this language in this decision compare to the waiver that you were made to sign before leaving Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, is the witness a jurist? Is he capable of discussing these kind of issues? There is no single word in those provisions that pertains to this witness. What is at stake here is abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What I understand the question to be, Mr. Krgovic - and Mr. Olmsted would certainly indicate whether we have it wrong - is that this being part of the law and, therefore, applicable to everyone, how does this --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one moment. We're not receiving a B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is it better -- is it up now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Keep talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- this particular provision, being part of the law library -- still not getting it? It's okay. Thank you. This particular provision, being part of the law library, is an item which is of general application and presumably known to everyone, hence the -- in terms of Mr. Krgovic's first objection about it being not shown to the witness not -- the fact that it wasn't, doesn't prohibit Mr. Olmsted from using it. And the question, as I understand - as I said, Mr. Olmsted would correct me if I misunderstand the import of his question - is: Having regard to this general provision, how did the waiver compare or how did it fit into this? Was -- was that your question, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Precisely. I couldn't have said it better myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, I trust you understand the -- Mr. Olmsted's question. If you're able to answer, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is the right question and a genuine confirmation of what I said earlier when I stated that for anyone to be able to leave Banja Luka they had to collect a number of documents required. And eventually, once these documents are filed, he, in turn, would be issued a document called a resettlement paper, which clearly states that every person leaving Banja Luka shall waiver the right to his mobile and immobile property. This decision was passed by the Crisis Staff, and it confirms verbatim what I've just told you. You can see here that they are taking over and disposing of the property in question. So what I said earlier is confirmed by this decision. And what I said was absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, at this point it might be appropriate for the Chamber to advise you of how your testimony has been understood. Because, in your answers to the questions put to you by Mr. Krgovic, you seemed to imply that what you signed off in relation to your property was not the legal ownership but, rather, the right to temporarily occupy and use the two houses, so as to allow the authorities in Banja Luka to use your houses for the purpose of resettling refugees. So there is a remaining question: Whether what you meant to say was the physical possession of your house on a temporary basis, or whether you were speaking about the legal ownership. And this is why counsel for the Prosecution is now raising the issue again. And if I may suggest to you that you either say that you don't know for sure, because you are not certain about the legal distinction. Or you repeat what you have said in your answers to counsel for the Defence; namely, that what you signed off was the -- the right to -- to use your property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So what I have just told you, sir, was meant to indicate you to the uncertainty that -- that may still remain in relation to your testimony. And I understand perfectly well that for someone who is not a trained lawyer the distinction between possession, on the one hand, and legal ownership, on the other hand, may not always be easy to -- to understand. So could I now direct you to inform the Chamber about your understanding of what it was that you signed off in those documents to the State of Republika Srpska at the time you left, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I left in 1993, I said that one had to have a final document called the resettlement paper. Its very name indicates that the person holding it is resettling and leaving the particular town and the part of the country where he or she used to live. The text contained in the resettlement paper makes no mention of temporary use. There is no word "temporary." Which means that my property that I was relinquishing was to be handed over to the state for its imposal [as interpreted]. Whether the state transferred the ownership in the land register is something that I said I know nothing about, because I wasn't there. But I can confirm -- and by the way, there are tens of thousands such settlement papers held by all the people who had to leave. You can check that it clearly states that our property was placed at the disposal and that the ownership of that property was taken over by the state. I only added that this decision of the Crisis Staff confirms this because it was them who disposed of the property, including mine. I left this to the municipality, and you yourselves know that a municipality was a basic organisational unit in our society. So it was not taken away temporarily. However, whether it was conducted properly, in a legal way, like a probate, I don't know. Maybe the people present here can help me with that. I hope I was clear in my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think this is as far as we can take the issue. But I leave -- give the floor back to you, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At page 3 of the transcript today, you were asked some questions about an incident in which the wall near your house was hit by an explosive device. And you testified that a police officer who was present told you that this was normal. To your knowledge, did the police ever conduct an investigation into this crime?

utterances.speaker: ST-223
utterances.text: Not that I know of. Because they considered this to be normal. And it was normal. Because we were able to collect pieces of such shells all around our neighbourhood. They even left one such device in front of my house. Maybe I omitted to mention that in my previous statement. So they actually left a Zolja with a grenade attached to it. And when I reported this to the international forces, they came and carried out a controlled explosion of that device in broad daylight. This is the truth, and everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also testified, in response to questions by Mr. Krgovic, that you believed that the police had to do something to stop all these crimes against the non-Serb population. Did you have a personal experience with your private business that led you to believe that the authorities in Banja Luka were co-operating with these criminal groups that were causing these problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object to all this. I mean, what's the point? Ask a question and now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, that objection was quite foreseeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And now that we're in open session, I repeat that the witness is released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- it is 1.20. I don't suppose the Prosecution has another witness that they intended to begin today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The only other witness we have in town is ST-008. He's still hospitalised, and there may be a further follow-up procedure necessary. So he will not be able to testify today or tomorrow. We have no other witness for the rest of this week. We have a full week, full slate of witnesses for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any procedural issues or housekeeping matters which need or could be dealt with before we rise for the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had one I wanted to bring to your attention before -- because it concerns the witness coming on Monday. And I think Mr. Zecevic has one. Now, mine, in regards to Witness ST-247, who's scheduled to testify Monday, by an oral ruling on the 11th of November, you admitted some of his testimony and gave us a certain time-limit. The question we needed clarification on was that by your oral ruling you indicated that the -- only the accompanying documents to his transcript that you found pertinent could be used. He has a transcript which highlighted in blue pertaining to the adjudicated fact and highlighted in yellow for other information we thought was relevant and pertinent as far as background and placing the adjudicated fact in context. It wasn't clear from the oral ruling whether all the yellow and all the blue is permitted and which accompanying documents. In your oral ruling you indicated that there would be written reasons to follow. And as far as I'm informed by Mr. Rindi, who's leading the witness, we haven't seen those written reasons yet for that witness. So if we could have that before Monday, it would help in preparation. That's all I had for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I would only say that that is in process. And we fully -- we understand the urgency of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hannis, aren't we also expecting an answer, reply, on the motion to re-call 191, if I'm not wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not sure. I've lost track. I will check on that and see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I thought that was for today, expedited responses. Unless I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was supposed to be an oral response for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah, I thought that Ms. Korner had already given an oral response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My Case Manager is looking at the transcript at page 17 -- I'm sorry. Give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pages 17946. She did give an oral response at that time, and I have nothing further to add to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's a couple of housekeeping matters. And there is our exhumation submission, additional exhumation submission. And I believe I will be able to deal with all of that in 20 minutes, if it pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order that we use the time efficiently. The first thing, Your Honours, the housekeeping matters. The day after the ST-041, the last witness for the Doboj municipality, was called, we received the batch 160, the disclosure from the Office of the Prosecutor. This disclosure, the batch 160, contains a number, precisely 24 documents, which are, to our opinion, extremely important, and -- and definitely severely impaired our -- our ability to cross-examine the witness, especially on the issues that the witness -- that that particular witness, ST-041, testified about. Now, we had this experience before, but it wasn't such a big problem because we always had another witness from the same region and we could use these documents. Now this -- this situation has created a problem for us because there are no more Doboj witnesses. I -- I just wanted to inform the Trial Chamber, we will try to find -- find out the solution by communicating to our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, but I just wanted to raise this with Your Honours. And it -- it creates a grave concern for us. Now the second thing, Your Honours. We -- I found out only yesterday watching the -- the live feed from the Status Conference of one of the -- in the other cases that -- that there is another enormous amount of documents, the military documents, the so-called Pecanac disclosure, it only came to my attention yesterday, then I checked and I hear that this enormous amount of documents has been disclosed to other Defence teams in other cases. In our case, we -- we never heard anything about it before yesterday. Now, it come to my -- when I started investigating that, I found out that there is -- there is four DVDs containing total of 6.662 documents. I know -- out of this number, the large number pertains to the -- to the documents which are outside the relevant period for this indictment. But just by -- just by shuffling through the list of the documents, I -- I identified at least one -- or let's say 10 per cent of the documents might be really relevant for us. Now, we sent the -- the mail to our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor immediately, when I found out about this -- this Pecanac disclosure. Now, this might -- this might, again, impair our ability to -- to cross-examine the -- the military expert in January, if we don't receive that on the -- on the -- on an expedited basis. And, plus, we need to know if there are any other documents in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor which have any military significance so that we know that once it is over and that we can really start preparing the cross-examination properly for the military expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Just to be clear about this Pecanac disclosure. Does it have the quality of being exculpatory material? Or is it just material that might be relevant or interesting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry I wasn't precise enough. These documents that I have been able to identify just by the list -- because I never saw the documents, you see, Your Honours, I just saw the list of the documents. And from that list, I -- it appears to me that the number of documents are 68 -- Rule 68 documents definitely, and the others are 66, Rule 66 documents. And we asked the Office of the Prosecutor to disclose that to us. Of course, they have the obligation to disclose the Rule 68 documents immediately. And it apparently is the situation that exists already one month ago. I wasn't aware. I'm really sorry, it might be -- it might be really my problem or my -- my mistake, that I didn't check the other cases. But, believe me, Your Honours, I don't have enough time for this particular case, not only to check what is happening in the other cases. So -- again, I -- we ask the Office of the Prosecutor to disclose that to us. We hope we will receive that. But I just wanted to raise this issue again with the Trial Chamber because we are concerned with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, are you able to shed some light over this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- not very much. Actually, Mr. Zecevic told me today he was going to make a submission on exhumations, and I didn't know this matter was coming up. This collection, I saw an e-mail at -- just this morning. I'm not sure who provided this to us. It appears to be mostly military material, but I have just now, while we were sitting here this morning, downloaded an Excel spreadsheet into my own collection so I can start a personal review on it. But as we stand here now, I can't tell you much more about it. Where it came from, how we got it, whether any of it is duplication of other materials, how much of it applies to 1992; I just don't know. All I can tell Your Honours right now is that after I leave the courtroom and take care of two other matters needing attention today, I will direct my attention to the Pecanac materials. And that's all I can tell Mr. Zecevic at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand and I appreciate it, because it just came up last night and this morning. Now, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But before we leave this issue, is anyone able to tell us just what the Pecanac documents are? I mean, have they recently been seized by the Prosecution or what -- what are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my understanding is that Mr. Pecanac was a high-ranking officer of the VRS and apparently was in a -- in a -- in a close surrounding to General Mladic. And the seizure of the documents is -- it's -- it's called Pecanac disclosure, Pecanac batch. So my assumption is that it was found somewhere in -- in the -- in the belonging of this officer. That is as far as I know at this moment, Your Honours, because, as I said, it only came yesterday evening to my attention that it exists at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just to be precise on my exhumations submissions, I will speak in Serbian language. [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to remind you that on the 17th of September of this year, on page 14822 of the transcript and onwards, Ms. Korner, Mr. Pantelic, and I presented our arguments related to exhumations. I would like to take this opportunity to incorporate all the arguments presented at the time in relation to this issue in order to avoid unnecessary repetition. On that occasion, I would like to remind you all again that we presented arguments regarding the position of the Prosecution that it is admissible at this phase of the proceedings for the Prosecution to expand its list by an additional 1.795 victims not listed in the schedule to the indictment. This was opposed by both Defence teams, and the Trial Chamber is to take a position on this, as far as we know. Your Honours, I sent copy of my submission to the interpreters in order to facilitate their work and in order to speed up this as much as possible. On that occasion, Your Honours, the Stanisic Defence informed the Trial Chamber that it officially asked the Prosecution for relevant documentation relating to 1.443 victims listed in the schedules to the indictment. On that occasion, in its response to the Defence arguments, Ms. Korner, on page 14834, claimed that at her request she would send the Defence all the necessary documentation relating to the victims, because this documentation is in the possession of the Prosecution, and if the Defence were to challenge these facts, which is the right of the Defence, the Prosecution was prepared to present necessary evidence. I will also like to remind you that the Defence informed the Trial Chamber, at the time that it asked the Prosecution to provide for each of the victims listed in the schedule to the indictment, only six basic pieces of information, and in the cases of missing persons, additional information declaring the missing person dead in accordance with the valid legal regulations and in a legal procedure before the Court. That was on page 14832. This necessary data was listed for the record. Indeed, on 18 October, in batch 151, the Prosecution provided the Defence, in an electronic format, the documentation which allegedly contained the requested information. Despite some technical difficulties, the Defence managed to analyse the supplied documentation. What we managed to establish is that this voluminous documentation contains information for over 9.000 alleged victims, that is, names. Victims between 1991 and 1995. This information is composed of several various databases in which the information was repeated and where some of the sought information was located. The problem is, Your Honours, that the documents on which the entries are based in these databases were not there, at least they were not given to us. Therefore, in our opinion, it is impossible to verify the veracity of the information in the database which was the essence of our request for disclosure. Our intention was to further clarify the situation, so we organised a meeting at the OTP with Ms. Alison Kipp who, as far as we know, is responsible in the OTP for maintaining this database. On that occasion we established that the Prosecution receives the information on alleged sources from -- victims from six sources which are listed in the database that the Prosecution initially offered on the 22nd of July. Back on 17th of September -- and I would like to repeat that in our opinion some of these sources are absolutely not objective. Furthermore, as we understood Ms. Kipp, the Prosecution receives databases from these sources which it simply copies into its own base without comparing the information and without verifying this information. Therefore, there is a certain number of duplicates for the same victims received from different sources. And, as far as we understood, the data entered into the database was mainly not verified. What we also managed to find out during the meeting is that these sources which provide the databases to the Prosecution only very rarely provide the Prosecution with documents on the basis of which these entries were made. So the Prosecution, in fact, has a very limited number of such documents. Perhaps, in our estimate, as little as 30 per cent, if as much. These are mainly forensic exhumation reports or death certificates without listing any further information about the time, the place, the mechanism of the source of the injury, et cetera. That is to say, after the Prosecution receives this information from the sources, it does not verify its accuracy, nor does it receive any supporting documentation which would indicate how these organisations got the information on a certain person being dead or missing. In particular, Your Honours, there's a certain significant number of persons who are in the Prosecution's database, and data about them is not furnished from either one of these six sources but that data is entered on the basis of witness statements which the Prosecution heard during the years of investigations. A consequence of such an approach is the further duplication of victims, because these -- this data is not compared with data received from other sources. On the basis of all of the above, we have the impression, Your Honours, that the Prosecution, in spite of their willingness to accommodate us, simply does not have all of the basic data about each of the victims which the Defence requested. Or if they do possess such data, then they don't possess the documents on the basis of which the data was entered into the database. During the meeting, we tried to reinforce our positions by picking at random one person from the database. Then we asked Ms. Kipp to find us the relevant data for that person. After 15 minutes of work, of searching, Ms. Kipp did not succeed in this task. This simply, in our opinion, means that the Defence, for the bulk of the victims, has no way of verifying the basis or the accuracy of the data entered into the OTP database. Your Honours, I would like to let the Chamber know that the Defence is continuing to analyse the documentation and is trying to establish what is missing, as well as the number of double entries for the same persons. But this task, in view of our resources, will take some time. To conclude, Your Honours, Ms. Korner and I have cited the jurisprudence of this Court supporting our requests stated on 17th of September, and I'm very briefly going to repeat three key positions in legal practice which I believe are relevant. It's a fact that a large number or a number of Trial Chambers of this Tribunal takes the position that the further the accused is removed from the crime itself, it is justified not to identify the victims to the extent and the degree required in cases of direct perpetrators. However, there are significant exceptions here. For example, in the Halilovic case, even though the accused was quite removed by the -- his function, from the very crime, the Trial Chamber insisted that the OTP identify beyond a reasonable doubt all the victims and the alleged perpetrators of the crimes, which, as is stated in the judgement, is something the OTP did not manage to do, which resulted in an acquittal. Two, even the Trial Chambers which accept the position that the more an accused is removed from the victim justifies a lower threshold of identification of victims still firmly believe that a victim has to be identified in such a way that enables the Defence to dispute that these victims were really the victims of the crimes that their clients are being charged with. This is the -- a decision in the Prlic trial regarding preliminary submissions. The Appeals Chamber, in its most recent decision on this question in the Gotovina case pursuant to an interlocutory appeal of last January, granted the Defence appeal and returned it for review to the Trial Chamber, in essence, confirming the position that I have just stated before. In view of everything that I have stated, I would like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Defence in this position is not prepared nor is it able to stipulate the facts contained in the OTP's exhumation database. Thank you very much. And this concludes my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Obviously this is something that's going to have to be digested. And we expect that the Prosecution would themselves, having considered what you would have said, make a response as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would request the opportunity for us to make some kind of response. Ms. Pidwell and Ms. Korner are the ones who've been dealing with this issue. But the bottom line is that the Defence is unable to stipulate, and therefore we think you've heard enough of the legal submissions about it, and we need a ruling on the -- whether or not you will grant our request to add the proof-of-death database. Because if you do, that settles one thing. If you decide that you cannot or will not, then we may have to make an application to the Court to try and deal with that evidence in some other fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic -- sorry, Mr. Zecevic. I'm sorry. You said that -- I'm going to repeat. You said: "... three key positions in legal practice which I believe are relevant." And then you said, "first." And you said "two." And I don't see "three." Did you miss something? Did I miss something? Or is it just a 1, 2, 3 that isn't clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will -- I will briefly try to explain, Your Honours. The first was the -- was the overwhelming position of the -- of the Trial Chambers concerning the -- the proximity of the accused and the crime. The second was the decision in Prlic on preliminary motions. The decision in case Prlic on preliminary motions where the Trial Chamber said that the victim must be identified in a manner that gives the opportunity to Defence to challenge that it's a victim of that crime. And the last was the appeals in Gotovina, the appeals decision in Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just have a question. It will take up two minutes. I thought I would have enough time to open it later. It's relating to Witness ST-260. We received an e-mail from the OTP yesterday when we asked to speak to the witness that the witness had informed the OTP that he was willing to speak to the Defence only if this was something that was granted by the Trial Chamber or was an instruction from the Trial Chamber. We know that this perhaps is not strictly something the Trial Chamber should do, but in view of the request by the witness, we are asking for further instructions. Should the Trial Chamber grant that the -- that the witness should speak to the Defence, or is there some other way that we could deal with it? But, anyway, this is information that we received from the OTP, and it was their suggestion that we bring this matter before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: With respect, I find that suggestion odd, because we have walked this road before and we have clearly stated it is not for the Trial Chamber to direct or suggest to -- the witness speaks to the other side. It's entirely up to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, I would ask the OTP to explain that to the witness, because evidently there is a communication problem. Or perhaps we can have the witness's contacts so that we can speak to him directly and put our position to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Or perhaps VWS could explain to the witness what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I can indicate, Your Honour, I have explained the position. I'm willing to do it again. And I'm happy for VWS to do it as well. Or instead of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we're five minutes past the time for adjournment. The -- we thank you the interpreters and the support staff for their indulgence. And we rise for the day. I wish everyone a safe weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
